name: Whey Protein
lead: Whey protein is a mixture of proteins isolated from whey, the liquid by-product of cheese making. Its main components are beta-lactoglobulin, alpha-lactalbumin, serum albumin and immunoglobulins, and it is sold mainly as a powdered protein supplement in concentrate, isolate and hydrolysate forms.[1]

It is used chiefly to support muscle growth and recovery after resistance training. A 2018 meta-analysis of 49 trials with 1,863 participants found that protein supplementation during prolonged resistance training modestly increased strength, fat-free mass and muscle size, with smaller effects on fat-free mass in older participants.[2] A 2024 network meta-analysis of 116 trials examined how timing and protein type affect results.[3] In 2010 a European Food Safety Authority panel concluded there was no evidence supporting weight-loss claims for whey and that it is roughly as effective as other protein sources for building strength and lean mass.[1]

Reviews of adverse effects associate chronic, excessive use with possible kidney, liver, acne and microbiota concerns, while other researchers have argued that some of these claims are unsubstantiated.[4][5]
infobox: By-product of cheese production; about 20% of cow's milk protein [1]
Soluble whey protein for beverages from 1969-1971 [1]

paras: Whey is the liquid left when milk is coagulated with acid or rennet. Protein is concentrated mainly by membrane filtration (microfiltration then ultrafiltration, followed by spray-drying) or ion-exchange chromatography.[1]

Whey protein concentrates retain some lactose and fat; isolates are processed to exceed 90 percent protein by dry weight; hydrolysates are partially pre-digested and costlier; native whey is taken from skim milk and lacks glycomacropeptide.[1] Wikipedia says whey appears more bioavailable than casein or soy protein.[1]

Lifters use whey shakes to reach daily protein targets, as a meal supplement or snack during cutting diets, and after training. T Nation logs show protein shakes added to meal plans and used in place of meals in diet phases.[6][7]

Whey is studied for sarcopenia (age-related muscle loss), often combined with leucine, vitamin D or exercise, and in clinical nutrition.[8][9][10][11] Hydrolysed whey is used in hypoallergenic infant formulas, though whey proteins are responsible for some milk allergies, with caseins the major allergens.[1]

The 2018 meta-analysis reported mean increases with protein supplementation of 2.49 kg in one-repetition-maximum strength and 0.30 kg in fat-free mass, plus gains in muscle fibre and mid-femur cross-sectional area, with effects diminishing with age and with higher baseline protein intake.[2] The 2024 network meta-analysis found that post-exercise and night-time protein supplementation improved fat-free mass, skeletal muscle mass or handgrip strength versus placebo.[3] Other meta-analyses examined recovery of muscle function, strength and body mass, and differences among concentrated, hydrolysed and isolated whey on body composition.[12][13][14]

In older adults, a one-year randomized trial examined daily protein supplementation with or without resistance training on muscle size, strength and function; the PROVIDE trial and other trials tested vitamin D and leucine-enriched whey in sarcopenia, and meta-analyses address whey with or without vitamin D or resistance training.[8][9][10][11][15]

A 2020 randomized trial compared whey and pea protein for post-eccentric exercise muscle damage.[16] A 2024 double-blind randomized equivalence trial examined whey protein and male acne.[17] An allergy task-force review examined dietary interventions for atopic dermatitis skin symptoms in children.[18]

A 2021 systematic review of 11 documents concluded that most papers linked damaging effects to chronic and excessive whey use, mainly in kidneys and liver, with other studies reporting associations with aggression, acne and microbiota changes, aggravated by sedentary lifestyle.[4] A published discussion of that review argued that claims of adverse effects of whey on kidney and liver function were unsubstantiated.[5]
Whey contains lactose in concentrates and is a milk allergen for some people.[1]

By the late 1960s surplus whey was an economic and environmental problem for the New Zealand dairy industry. In 1969 Coca-Cola Export Corporation executive Alex Malaspina asked the New Zealand Dairy Board for soluble whey protein for acidic carbonated drinks, which led to development of beverage-grade concentrate and to Tai, a whey-fortified drink launched by Coca-Cola in Brazil in 1971. By the late 1980s whey proteins were gaining importance in sports nutrition, weight management and medical nutrition.[1]
In lifting forums whey is a default supplement, mentioned in meal logs and as a convenient protein source, and appears in jokes about protein shakes.[6][7][19]

lore.intro: Whey is treated in physique communities as an ordinary protein source, with occasional debate over acne and kidney effects.[6][7]

claims.believers: Lifters add shakes to meal plans to hit protein goals during training.[6][7]
claims.experts: Meta-analyses report modest gains in strength and lean mass with protein supplementation, smaller in older and higher-intake groups; EFSA judged whey about as effective as other proteins.[1][2]

claims.believers: Shakes are used as meal replacements in cutting phases.[7]
claims.experts: The 2010 EFSA panel found no evidence supporting weight-loss claims.[1]

claims.believers: Users commonly report skin breakouts after starting shakes.
claims.experts: A systematic review lists acne among reported associations and a 2024 double-blind trial tested whey and male acne.[4][17]

claims.believers: Concern circulates around heavy protein use.
claims.experts: A 2021 review linked chronic abusive use to organ effects while a published discussion called such claims unsubstantiated.[4][5]
